Although the program runs without error, from “yearout” table it gives me an organism length that is much too long for my species. I have tried to mess around with the parameters to see if anything changes this and so far the only one that seems to make any significant difference is z.mult…but this doesn’t seem like the right way to solve the problem. messages.subject: Re: Final Length of Animal
parts:
Hi - the DEB parameter that converts structural lengths to physical lengths is 'del.M'. The z.mult parameter allows you to scale the organism up and down in size according to the DEB covariation rules (whereby size at birth, size at puberty, maximum size, egg size and longevity all scale together in a particular way).

But I don't think you need to change anything if you're aiming to simulate the Desert Tortoise. The length is in mm and represents plastron length in this case. If you play around with this app http://bioforecasts.science.unimelb.edu.au/app_direct/deb/ choosing the Desert Tortoise, you'll see it gives sensible lengths, as does the ectotherm function. Perhaps it was simply that you didn't realize it was mm? Or did you want to simulate a different species starting from the Desert Tortoise by altering parameters?

All the best,
Mike

Hi - the DEB parameter that converts structural lengths to physical lengths is 'del.M'. The z.mult parameter allows you to scale the organism up and down in size according to the DEB covariation rules (whereby size at birth, size at puberty, maximum size, egg size and longevity all scale together in a particular way).

If you play around with this app http://bioforecasts.science.unimelb.edu.au/app_direct/deb/ choosing the Desert Tortoise, you'll see it gives sensible lengths, as does the ectotherm function. Hi - the DEB parameter that converts structural lengths to physical lengths is 'del.M'. The z.mult parameter allows you to scale the organism up and down in size according to the DEB covariation rules (whereby size at birth, size at puberty, maximum size, egg size and longevity all scale together in a particular way).

If you play around with this app http://bioforecasts.science.unimelb.edu.au/app_direct/deb/ choosing the Desert Tortoise, you'll see it gives sensible lengths, as does the ectotherm function.
